problem: "before any law" is ambiguous (reads as temporal) for "in preference to any law"; "ordinary" added to "cannot be modified by a law".
replacement: In the United States the constitution binds the legislator just as it binds the private citizen. It is the first of laws, so it cannot be modified by a law, and it is only right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to any law. The power of the judiciary depends on this condition, because every magistrate has a natural right to choose the legal obligation that binds him most strictly.

problem: The "when I told them ... when I demonstrated" structure is broken: "So the king..." turns his "so that" result clause into a free-standing assertion; "once" added in the final sentence.
replacement: In the Year VIII of the French Republic a constitution was drawn up that included the following clause: “Art. 75. All the agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted for offenses relating to their several functions by virtue of a decree of the Conseil d’Etat; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary tribunals.” This clause outlasted the “Constitution de l’An VIII,” and it is still maintained in spite of the just complaints of the nation. I have always had the utmost difficulty explaining its meaning to Englishmen or Americans. They at once concluded that the Conseil d’Etat in France was a great tribunal, established in the center of the kingdom, exercising a preliminary and somewhat tyrannical jurisdiction in all political cases. But when I told them that the Conseil d’Etat was not a judicial body in the common sense of the term, but an administrative council made up of men dependent on the Crown, so that the king, after ordering one of his servants, called a Prefect, to commit an injustice, has the power to command another of his servants, called a Councillor of State, to prevent the first from being punished; when I showed them that a citizen injured by the sovereign’s order is obliged to ask the sovereign for permission to obtain redress, they refused to believe so flagrant an abuse and were tempted to accuse me of falsehood or ignorance. Before the Revolution it often happened that a Parliament issued a warrant against a public officer who had committed an offense, and sometimes the proceedings were stopped by the authority of the Crown, which enforced compliance with its absolute and despotic will. It is painful to see how much lower we have sunk than our forefathers, since we allow to pass, under the color of justice and the sanction of the law, things that only violence could impose.

problem: Causal "and so" added where the source only describes; "from a wish" became "by an effort".
replacement: Under absolute governments, extraordinary forms of procedure would serve no purpose. The prince in whose name an offender is prosecuted is as much the sovereign of the courts as of everything else, and the way people think of his power is security enough. His only fear is that the outward formalities of justice may be neglected, and that his authority may be dishonored from a wish to make it more absolute. But in most free countries, where the majority can never influence the courts as an absolute monarch does, judicial power has sometimes been placed for a time in the representatives of the nation. People have judged it better to confuse the functions of the different authorities for a while than to violate the necessary principle that government is one.
